content: Anaesthetic drugs administered during general anaesthesia are typically adjusted based on the patient’s physiological responses, such as changes in heart rate or movement in response to surgical stimuli. However, advancements in technology now allow for the measurement of anaesthetic depth using electroencephalography (EEG). One such EEG-based tool is the entropy monitor, which uses electrodes placed on the forehead to assess the depth of anaesthesia. This device can guide the administration of anaesthetic drugs during surgery. The primary aim of this review was to evaluate whether entropy monitoring facilitates faster recovery from general anaesthesia. Additionally, the review sought to assess mortality rates at 24 hours, 30 days, and one year after general anaesthesia when entropy monitoring was used. Secondary objectives included determining whether entropy monitoring reduces the risk of postoperative recall of intraoperative events (awareness), decreases the amount of anaesthetic drugs used, lowers the cost of anaesthesia, and shortens the time required for patients to be ready to leave the postanaesthesia care unit (PACU). The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving adults and children over the age of two. In these trials, one group of patients received anaesthesia titrated using entropy monitoring, while the control group received standard care based on physiological responses. Some trials also included a third group where another EEG-based monitor, the Bispectral Index (BIS), was used to assess anaesthetic depth. A total of 11 RCTs involving 962 participants were included in the review. Eight trials (762 participants) focused on adults aged 18 to 80 years, two trials (128 participants) involved children aged 2 to 16 years, and one trial (72 participants) included older adults aged 60 to 75 years. Of these studies, three were judged to have a low risk of bias, while the remaining eight had unclear or high risk of bias. Six RCTs (383 participants) evaluated the primary outcome of time to awakening after stopping general anaesthesia. The results showed that patients in the entropy monitoring group woke up faster than those in the standard care group, with a mean difference (MD) of -5.42 minutes (95% confidence interval [CI]: -8.77 to -2.08). However, there was variability in the results, particularly in studies involving major, long-duration surgeries such as off-pump coronary artery bypass grafting and major urological procedures. In contrast, studies involving shorter ambulatory procedures showed a smaller mean difference in awakening time of -3.20 minutes (95% CI: -3.94 to -2.45). No trials reported on mortality at 24 hours, 30 days, or one year. Eight trials (797 participants) examined the secondary outcome of postoperative recall of intraoperative events (awareness). Only one patient in the standard care group reported awareness, making it difficult to draw meaningful conclusions about the benefit of entropy monitoring in preventing awareness. All 11 RCTs compared the amount of anaesthetic agents used between the entropy monitoring and standard care groups. Six trials assessed propofol usage, four evaluated sevoflurane consumption, and one examined isoflurane usage. Analysis of three studies (166 participants) showed that propofol consumption was slightly lower in the entropy group, with a mean difference of -11.56 mcg/kg/min (95% CI: -24.05 to 0.92), but the evidence quality was low. Two studies (156 participants) found that sevoflurane consumption was reduced in the entropy group, with a mean difference of -3.42 mL (95% CI: -6.49 to -0.35), and the evidence quality was moderate. None of the trials reported on the cost of general anaesthesia. Three trials (170 participants) assessed the time to readiness to leave the PACU. The mean difference in time to readiness was -5.94 minutes (95% CI: -16.08 to 4.20), but the evidence quality was low. Variability in results was attributed to differences in anaesthetic techniques, with one study using propofol-based anaesthesia and the other two using volatile-based anaesthesia. When only the two volatile-based anaesthesia studies were analyzed, the mean difference in PACU readiness time was -4.17 minutes (95% CI: -6.84 to -1.51). In conclusion, the evidence supporting the benefits of entropy monitoring in reducing time to awakening, preventing intraoperative awareness, and decreasing the use of inhalational anaesthetic agents was of moderate quality. However, the evidence for reductions in intravenous anaesthetic agent (propofol) use and time to readiness to leave the PACU was of low quality. Further research with larger participant numbers is needed to confirm the potential benefits of entropy monitoring. Additionally, future studies should investigate its impact on short-term and long-term mortality, as well as the cost-effectiveness of general anaesthesia guided by entropy monitoring.
